newsitem.title: UK: Exchange merger potential seen in deregulated grain markets.
newsitem.headline: Exchange merger potential seen in deregulated grain markets.

text.p: Two of London's futures exchanges merged on Monday in the hope of providing a winning combination to take advantage of the less rigid farm policy across Europe.

Called a merger, it is effectively a takeover of the old London Commodity Exchange (LCE) by the much bigger and brasher London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) that the LCE helped father just over 15 years ago.

The physical delivery of most commodity markets was stressed in the catchphrase "LIFFE goes physical". LIFFE officials make no secret of their desire to provide farmers with a means of protecting themselves from unpredictable prices.
This ambition extends across the European Union (EU) into central and eastern Europe following the breakup of the former Soviet Union.

"LIFFE is determined to ensure that financial futures and options emerging as a result of EMU (European Monetary Union) are traded in London and that it becomes the world centre for Euro derivatives trading," said LIFFE chairman Jack Wigglesworth.

"In addition, the creation of a single trading complex in London allows the exchange to grasp the opportunities offered by freer agricultural markets in Europe and to offer the risk management facilities consumers and producers want," he added.
Before the merger was agreed, the LCE and Chicago's Board of Trade (CBOT) looked at a joint venture to trade grain in London in the European time zone.
This now comes off the backburner but Wigglesworth said a new wheat contract is unlikely to start trading before 1998.
With the merger LIFFE has inherited the LCE's wheat and barley futures contracts but only with delivery in Britain.
Strong global farmer response to high prices and falling stocks in the past 18 months has lifted the spectre of food shortages and grain prices have retreated.

Freer grain trade agreed under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade's (GATT) Uruguay round was aimed to boost grain output. But analysts said it can have a flip side in removing price protection in times of surplus.
Free trade removes the downside safety net for farmers when production is in surplus. LIFFE hopes its marketing skills will help it to exploit this uncertainty.
"Farmers are expected to continue to respond more rapidly to price signals in a more liberated market," said International Grain's Council (IGC) economist Bill de Maria.
"Governments are no longer willing to assume all the costs of stocks and are shifting responsibility for stockholding to the private sector," he added.
If an increasing amount of grain production is going to be subject to free market pressures then analysts say farmers will need futures markets that they can readily relate to.
One exchange official said although much is said about eastern European commodity trade and exchanges, many eastern traders are only just understanding trading concepts.
Comprehension of futures trading will take longer.
Recent government policy in most major grain exporters has favoured working with low stocks. Large stocks, controlled by high prices, previously buffered the world against poor crops.
Analysts said combining free trade with low stocks is nearly impossible without the addition of more volatile prices.

It is still far from clear whether this is something that was fully taken account of in the Uruguay Trade negotiations round when the GATT's international negotiators were concerned with farmers responding to shortages and growing more, rather than cutting back in the face of surpluses.
"It would not surprise me if we soon see farmers calling for protection if stocks build and prices fall," said one analyst.
Last week the U.S. Department of Agriculture forecast higher crops in most major producing areas as farmers planted more.

If the IGC follows the same trend when it updates its estimates next week, then world wheat and coarse grain stocks by the end of the 1996/97 seasons may be back to near 200 million tonnes, or up 10 percent in 12 months.
